extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations; public relations managers and educators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on managing the public relations function using role definitions, a systems management framework (functions, structures, processes, feedback), and contingency-based selection of models and structures according to environmental complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication technician
rubrics_metrics.description: These practitioners provide the communication and journalistic skills—writing, editing, audiovisual production, graphics, and production of messages—needed to carry out public relations programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communication technicians do not make organizational decisions. They implement the decisions of others, and do not do research to plan or evaluate their work. Examples of technician tasks: writing press releases, preparing audiovisual materials, producing an employee newspaper, writing speeches. In small organizations one person may fill many technical tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication manager
rubrics_metrics.description: These practitioners systematically plan and manage an organization’s public relations program, counsel management, and make communication policy decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communication managers are involved in all segments of PR decision making and frequently use research to plan or evaluate their work. At higher levels they plan the entire PR program, supervise middle managers, and counsel top managers on communication policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert prescriber (manager subrole)
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations manager sometimes functions as the 'expert' who researches and defines PR problems, develops programs, and takes responsibility for implementing programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is one of three manager subroles; it emphasizes developing and executing professional solutions rather than facilitating others' processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication facilitator (manager subrole)
rubrics_metrics.description: In this subrole the PR practitioner serves as a sensitive 'go-between' to keep continuous two-way communication flowing between the organization and its publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The facilitator acts as liaison, interpreter, and mediator, emphasizing sustained two-way exchange rather than top-down message delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-solving process facilitator (manager subrole)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PR manager helps others in the organization solve their public relations problems by involving members of other organizational subsystems (or client organizations) and helping them plan and implement their own PR programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This role emphasizes collaborative, process-oriented facilitation over prescription; useful when building internal capacity or working across units or in agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media-relations role
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who maintains contact with the media and keeps others in the organization informed about what the media are doing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media-relations people play a two-way symmetric role with the media—they do not just produce and disseminate messages but also listen and respond to media dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication liaison role
rubrics_metrics.description: The PR person represents the organization at events and meetings and creates opportunities for management to communicate with internal and external publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This role supports higher-level PR managers by representing organizational interests and facilitating management-public interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role development and career progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners should explore different roles during training; roles must change if a PR person is to advance through a career.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginning professionals typically start as communication technicians. To advance toward PRSA's professional-manager and senior-professional levels, individuals should learn management, planning, and evaluation (e.g., take business or public administration courses) and think beyond technician tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systems management is holistic
rubrics_metrics.description: The manager cannot think of an organization or department by itself; systems managers consider relationships between the organization and environmental systems and interdependence among organizational units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR managers must work with other subsystems to solve PR problems and recognize that many PR problems originate in the environment and require adaptation or control of interpenetrating systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systems management challenges established practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems managers aim not just to keep the organization running but to work with organizational and environmental subsystems to develop innovative solutions (a 'moving equilibrium').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR practitioners should change roles and develop new roles as problems and environments change; they may also advocate structural and policy changes when environmental systems perceive organizational irresponsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systems management is mission-oriented
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems managers know what they want to accomplish and systematically set out to accomplish it, constantly monitoring progress toward goals and objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formal management devices (MBO, PPBS, PERT) to focus on progress toward objectives; apply planning and budgeting systems to PR goals and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systems managers use quantitative methods and computers
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers gather and process information and then use computers and quantitative methods to help make decisions (manage via a Management Information System).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MIS and quantitative methods are becoming necessary for PR managers to demonstrate management capability comparable to other organizational departments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systems managers choose control/adapt strategy (control vs adapt vs both)
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers must decide whether to attempt to control other systems, adapt to other systems, or do both, depending on the organization's environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-way asymmetric managers tend toward attempting to control systems in the environment; two-way symmetric managers tend to adapt the organization to the environment or view both as interpenetrating systems and choose a mix of adaptation and control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core systems concepts: input, throughput, output, feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems receive informational inputs from the environment, process them (throughput) to formulate solutions, release outputs to the environment, and seek feedback to determine whether the problem is solved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the cycle iteratively until equilibrium is restored. For PR management, inputs are informational; throughput organizes information and develops interventions; outputs are PR actions; feedback evaluates impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reactive vs proactive behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Reactive systems wait for environmental inputs and then change; proactive systems begin with throughput by deliberately releasing outputs intended to change interpenetrating systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactive PR anticipates problems and deliberately shifts equilibrium by planned outputs, then handles the resulting environmental reactions. Choose proactive tactics when intentionally trying to reshape environments; be prepared to manage ensuing problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four management components to manage PR subsystem: functions, structures, processes, feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective PR managers must define (1) functions (what the subsystem does), (2) structures (how roles are organized), (3) processes (decision-making rules and procedures), and (4) feedback (mechanisms to learn the impact of outputs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
• Functions: choose the communication function appropriate to the PR model (propaganda/publicity; information; scientific persuasion; mutual understanding).
• Structures: choose vertical (superior–subordinate) and horizontal (division of technical tasks) arrangements to best deliver the chosen function; document via org charts and job descriptions.
• Processes: define who does what and how to handle inputs and produce outputs.
• Feedback: design feedback loops and seek informational inputs (beyond mere feedback) when using two-way symmetric models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select PR function/model contingent on environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers should decide what PR function (press agentry/publicity, public information, two-way asymmetric, two-way symmetric) will best serve the organization by examining the organization’s environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Static environments favor press agentry or public-information models (publicity/information). Dynamic, complex environments favor two-way asymmetric or symmetric models which provide feedback and allow controlling or adapting to environmental change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess environmental complexity using specific characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish static vs dynamic (complex) environments by characteristics such as changes in technology, extent of mechanization, stability of demand, amount of competition, degree of social/political support, and growth in relevant knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dynamic/complex environment (high tech change, high demand variability, substantial competition, volatile social/political support, rapid knowledge growth) requires more adaptive, research-based PR approaches (two-way models). Use Aldrich's characteristics—resource richness, homogeneity/heterogeneity, stability/instability, concentration/dispersion—to further analyze environmental demands and opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose vertical and horizontal structures to implement functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers must choose both vertical structure (superior–subordinate relationships) and horizontal structure (division of work across units) to provide the chosen PR function effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horizontal structure may assign technical tasks (e.g., press releases vs annual reports) to specialized groups. Structure choice should align with required function and environmental contingencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way models differ in input usage (feedback-only vs informational inputs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-way asymmetric PR practitioners rely primarily on feedback as environmental input (produce outputs then seek reactions), whereas two-way symmetric practitioners seek informational inputs other than feedback (research before action) and then use feedback to evaluate programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using two-way symmetric approaches, build research into planning so programs are informed by publics' likely reactions; use feedback for evaluation and iterative improvement.
